This War of Mine approaches armed conflict from a perspective that remains unusual in gaming: the people who are simply trying to stay alive while a city collapses around them. Developed and published by 11 bit studios, it places the player in charge of a small group of civilians trapped during a siege. There are no heroic military campaigns or promises of glorious victory. Instead, survival depends on finding food, keeping the shelter warm, treating wounds, managing exhaustion, and making difficult choices when there are not enough resources to satisfy everyone’s needs.

The gameplay is divided between daytime shelter management and nighttime expeditions. During the day, venturing outside is too dangerous, so survivors remain inside their damaged refuge. This is when players search the building, prepare meals, construct equipment, improve defenses, treat illness, rest exhausted characters, and decide how limited materials should be spent. Building a stove, bed, heater, workshop, rainwater collector, or other useful equipment can substantially improve the group’s chances, but every project consumes resources that might be desperately needed elsewhere. This creates a strong economy of scarcity in which even basic materials retain importance throughout much of a campaign.

Night changes the rhythm dramatically. One survivor can be sent to scavenge while the others remain behind to sleep or guard the shelter. The selected scavenger visits locations ranging from abandoned buildings to dangerous areas occupied by soldiers, criminals, traders, or desperate civilians. Limited carrying capacity forces constant decisions about what is valuable enough to bring home. Medicine might save a sick companion, food can prevent starvation, components allow essential upgrades, and valuables can be traded later. Finding useful supplies is only part of the problem because the character must also survive long enough to return with them.

Combat exists, but treating it as the primary solution is usually a mistake. Civilians are vulnerable, weapons can be difficult to obtain, and injuries may require supplies the shelter cannot afford to lose. Stealth, observation, distraction, avoidance, and careful timing can be far more effective. The danger of violence gives hostile encounters genuine tension because a poorly judged confrontation can permanently alter an otherwise promising campaign.

The moral dimension is where the game becomes considerably more than a conventional survival-management experience. Supplies can sometimes be stolen from people who need them just as badly as your own group. A stranger may ask for assistance when you can barely feed your existing survivors. Someone vulnerable might possess medicine that could save one of your companions. The game rarely presents these situations as obvious good-or-evil choices. Instead, it asks what people are prepared to sacrifice when compassion itself becomes expensive.

Survivors also have distinct personalities, strengths, weaknesses, and emotional responses. They are not merely interchangeable workers represented by numerical statistics. A character may be a particularly useful scavenger, cook, negotiator, or guard, while another may struggle more severely with traumatic actions. Hunger, sickness, wounds, tiredness, and psychological deterioration all need attention. A physically healthy survivor can still become dangerously depressed after witnessing death or participating in cruel actions. This connection between practical survival and emotional well-being gives individual characters greater significance.

Randomized circumstances strengthen replayability. Available survivors, locations, events, shortages, weather conditions, and other factors can change the way a campaign develops. A strategy that produces a comfortable shelter in one run may collapse when circumstances are less favorable in another. Winter can turn fuel into a critical concern, raids may punish inadequate defenses, and unexpected illness can consume medicine intended for emergencies. The best moments frequently occur when several problems appear simultaneously and the player has to decide which crisis can be temporarily ignored.

The visual direction remains one of its defining qualities. Environments have a rough, charcoal-like appearance that suits the destroyed city and creates the impression of wartime illustrations brought to life. Buildings are displayed through a cutaway perspective, allowing players to navigate individual floors and rooms while maintaining a claustrophobic feeling. Muted colors, darkness, weather, ruined architecture, and restrained animation reinforce the bleak atmosphere without requiring excessive visual spectacle. The soundtrack and environmental audio similarly favor tension and melancholy rather than action-oriented excitement.

The expanded Final Cut version makes the overall experience richer by incorporating years of additions and improvements. Additional scenarios, characters, locations, quests, and content broaden the possible situations players can encounter. The Stories expansions push the concept further toward structured storytelling, exploring subjects such as family, loss, information, responsibility, and cultural preservation. These additions fit naturally because they examine different dimensions of civilian existence during conflict rather than simply providing more weapons or easier methods of survival.

There are frustrations. Character movement can occasionally feel cumbersome, particularly when precise actions are required during dangerous scavenging missions. Random events may create situations where careful preparation still ends badly, and the early learning process can be unforgiving. The deliberately slow pace will not appeal to players looking for constant action. Its oppressive atmosphere can also become emotionally exhausting, especially across longer sessions. These characteristics are important considerations rather than insignificant flaws.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Playable rather than Verified. The core experience can be played on Steam Deck, but users should expect some compromises compared with games specifically optimized for Valve’s handheld. Certain interactions or interface elements may be less comfortable on the smaller display, so players seeking a completely seamless handheld experience should keep the Playable classification in mind.

Ultimately, This War of Mine remains compelling because virtually every system contributes to its central theme. Crafting is about keeping vulnerable people alive, scavenging is driven by necessity, combat carries consequences, and moral choices can affect both immediate survival and psychological stability. It turns mundane accomplishments such as preparing enough food, finding medicine, surviving a freezing night, or returning safely from a scavenging trip into meaningful victories. Its uncompromising treatment of civilian survival gives it an identity few games have successfully replicated.

Rating: 9/10

This game is an excellent blend of stealth, resource management, base building and decision making. You play as a group of civilians trapped in a city beseiged by an ongoing war. Scavenge, trade, craft and even lie and kill your way to survival. The question is, how far would you go to survive? This War of Mine asks this question constantly, and it means it.

One highlight is how good the game is in connecting you with your survivors. I have felt despair, anguish, sadness and hope in my playthroughs. It's remarkable how the game accomplishes this although each playthough can be very differerent. The game sets you up with a different set of survivors each time you play, and many events and locations are randomly generated to a certain extent. You may see the same location in a subsequent playthrough but the events and circumstances might be different, prompting you to use a different strategy whist visiting. A market square bustled with survivors eagerly engaging in black market trade might become a dangerous, deserted spot preyed upon by hostile snipers in your next game.

I thoroughly enjoyed my time with This War of Mine. Everything feels fresh and new, and I feel I'm a kid again eagerly discovering everything for the first time. This is the sleeper hit of the year.

Solid premise and fine execution, but deep flaws in the mechanics that make me not want to return to this game. For example, why am I unable to send out multiple people to scavenge at once if I want? The day ends at 8pm sharp, and if your character hasn't eaten yet by that time because you forgot or something, your character will just starve until the next day because I guess everyone sleeps at 8pm through the night. 
Character moods/relationships need a rework. One character was dying of a terminal illness, so I sent my other character to rob medicine from a hospital, but the dying character only said something like "How could she rob a hospital?" No gratefulness for saving his life. I've read on the wiki there are multiple endings that hinges on arbitrary choices made throughout the game, so even if you survive and are healthy, the game may not deem you worthy of a good ending. Just too many design choices that leave me frustrated at why wasn't more player choice given.

This War of Mine makes you realise the terrible nature of war better than a thousand ad-campaigns can.

Very impressive game!

I’ve actually been curious about This War of Mine for a long time, but only recently got the chance to play it, and well... it surprised me in ways I didn’t expect. The game completely shifted the way I see war and conflict. Instead of focusing on soldiers or heroic battles, it forces you to experience everything through the eyes of ordinary civilians who are just trying to survive.

Every in-game day feels heavy. It’s not just about finding food or medicine, but about holding on to your humanity when everything around you is falling apart. Even small choices can leave you feeling guilty or unsure, and that emotional weight really stayed with me, especially that time when i forced to robe that elder couple's house. 

This game made me realize that war isn’t just about tactics or glory, it’s about people whose lives are torn apart without warning.

War is raging outside...

First few days for us weren't that bad considering the circumstances. Pavle found heaps of materials, spare parts, wood. Pretty soon we were able to fortify our home. We grew accustomed to it. In the beginning we got raided on what felt like a regular basis. And they always went for the food and water. It got tougher. 

Everyday we listened to the radio. Gotta know what's going on out there, right? Radio has been telling us about an increasing rate of crimes and robberies. No shit, Sherlock...
We got hungry. Then we got very hungry. Night came and again our home was chosen for a raid. But not this time. We closed every hole in our walls and we were armed - well we had a shovel - but it worked. We managed to fend of our first raid. Things were looking up. Then it drew on us. What good is all our wood, fortification and our shovel, if we can't eat. 

We've scavenged quite a few locations by now. Always came back with our backpacks filled to the brim, but lacking food and water. We grew sad. One of us grew ill. We gave him some medication and let him sleep it off. The rest of us sat down on our two armchairs around our radio, listening to classical music. It felt strange to sit on those comfy armchairs, fancy music echoing from the walls, while we were lacking the bare essentials. My stomach rumbled, then somebody knocked on the door.

It was a woman, self proclaimed singer. A cheery girl in a good physical condition. She asked if she could stay with us. We weren't even able to feed three people but hell, I liked her. We let her stay with us. She might be able to lift our spirits. A good girl she was.

Night came once more. With all of us quite shaken up from the dire situation, we sent the new girl out to scavenge. The other three of us were close to starvation. What happened then, is what the new girl told us the next morning. 
While we fended off yet another raid, she did...well, what had to be done. You know, there was this lonely elderly couple living just a few blocks from us. Our new girl visited them. They asked her to leave, to spare their food. They begged her. When she began ransacking through their stuff, they fled to the attic. Waiting for everything to be over. We took their food, took their water. Even took some jewelry for bartering later down the road. We did not take their medical supplies...they would need them pretty soon...thanks to what we took from them. 

Next day the new girl told us about that night while we ate our first cooked meal in days. We were still hungry. What have we done? Depression took the better part of us and we spent the day together around the radio - comforting each other. That night, everybody stayed at home. Everybody slept.

Couple of days later, things are not as bad. We're still kinda sad and food is an ongoing issue, but we managed to build a device to collect and filter rainwater and we caught our first small animals to fight the hunger. Supply around town is running low though and we need to take bigger risks. We built knives. Everyone of us has one now. Our home stands. Each night one of us is going out there to provide for the group. Until now, they've always returned. And until now, only once, we had to do the bad thing. Until now...
